lesson.title: Reading the Verdict
lesson.summary: Homogeneity and independence conclusions follow the same three-part template and identical underlying arithmetic, but they use genuinely different wording, distribution across groups versus association between variables, that must not be mixed up.
lesson.body:
By this point, homogeneity and independence tests have used the exact same tools: the same chi-square formula, the same row total times column total, divided by grand total expected count formula, the same rows minus 1 times columns minus 1 degrees of freedom, and the same large counts condition. What still needs care is the very last step, translating a P-value into a conclusion, because homogeneity and independence conclusions are worded differently even when the numbers behind them are identical.

Every chi-square conclusion, homogeneity or independence, follows the same three-part shape used throughout this course: compare the P-value to the significance level, state a decision about H0, and restate that decision in the context of the original question.

For the homogeneity example, study preference across three schools, the statistic was X squared is approximately 3.42 with 4 degrees of freedom, giving a P-value of roughly 0.49. Since 0.49 is far larger than a standard alpha of 0.05, we fail to reject H0. In context: we do not have convincing evidence that the distribution of study preference differs among students at these three schools.

For the independence example, exercise frequency and sleep quality, the statistic was X squared is approximately 24.09 with 2 degrees of freedom, giving a P-value of roughly 0.000006. Since that is far smaller than 0.05, we reject H0. In context: we have convincing evidence of an association between exercise frequency and sleep quality among the adults sampled.

Notice the difference in vocabulary even though the surrounding logic is identical: the homogeneity conclusion talks about a distribution being the same or different across groups, while the independence conclusion talks about an association existing or not existing between two variables within one population. Mixing up that vocabulary, even with a perfectly correct chi-square statistic, is a common way to lose credit on this kind of conclusion.

A rejected H0, in either kind of test, only says that something is going on somewhere in the table, not exactly where. Revisiting the individual observed minus expected, squared, over expected terms is how you dig into that further. In the sleep and exercise example, the Good sleep and Rarely exercise cell contributed about 6.94 and the Good sleep and Regular exercise cell contributed about 6.26 to the total of 24.09, the two largest pieces, hinting that regular exercisers reported good sleep more often than a no-association model would predict, while those who rarely exercise reported good sleep less often than predicted. That is a useful follow-up observation, but it is descriptive, not part of the formal test itself.

Finally, keep the causation caveat straight. An independence test built on an observational sample, like the adults surveyed on exercise and sleep, can only support association language, never causal language, no matter how small the P-value gets. A homogeneity test can support causal language only if the groups themselves were formed by random assignment in a genuine experiment. When the groups are instead pre-existing populations sampled independently, as with the three schools, differs across groups is exactly as far as the conclusion can honestly go.
